_readme: The three missions the player can choose: Moon, Mars and Venus (PLAN.md section 5). Each one is a place AND a goal. Every fact is written as { "value": ..., "source": ... } so you can see where it came from. A source is a link to NASA, a written game-design choice, or the word PLACEHOLDER (made up for now; a student replaces it before the final submission). locked = true means the card shows but cannot be picked yet. arrival_type = how the trip ends: "orbit" (circle the planet) or "surface" (land). crew = true if people travel with the spacecraft you build. goals = the ids of the success checklist; the sentences for each id are in data/story.json. limits_from = which mission in game_data.json ("missions") holds the budget, mass and other limits. The words on the screen (names, goals, descriptions) are in data/story.json. The card order on screen is the order in this file.

arrival._readme: The arrival walk (PLAN.md section 10). area = "plain" (walk on the ground) or "ship" (inside a ship). Sizes and positions are in meters: [x, y, z]; the player starts at player_start and looks toward -z. Colors are web color codes. fog_enabled / fog_density = the haze. gravity_scale = how strong gravity is compared with the game's normal (1 = normal). rock_* = random gray-box rocks (rock_seed = which random layout; rocks stay rock_keep_clear meters away from the lander and the spots). marker_* = the glowing floor marker on each spot. spots = the task places. tasks = the tasks in list order. Each task: type = reach (step on the spot), press (press E), hold (hold E, let go between green_start and green_end; the bar fills in fill_seconds; full is too far) or send (press E, then data goes home); needs_instrument = an instrument that must be packed; needs_tasks = tasks that must be done first; missing_finding = the report card when the instrument was not packed; data_gb = data a send task adds to the report. send = how long sending takes: base_seconds with a signal at the mission's communications limit, longer with a weaker one, at most max_seconds. goals = which tasks tick each checklist goal ("arrive" = ticked as soon as you arrive). Art pass (Step 13): lander leg_height / foil_color / leg_color / dish_color = legs, gold foil band and a dish; round_rocks = lumpy stones instead of boxes; hills = big low hills far away; stars = dots in the sky; spot_props = a prop next to a spot (kind console or dish, offset in meters); done_props = a prop that appears on the spot when that task is done (seismometer, drill_rig). Prop colors: game_data.json "arrival_props". Layout and look: game-design choices. hold, send and data_gb: PLACEHOLDER.
arrival._gravity_source: Real gravity jumps (team decision 2026-11-14): Mars' surface gravity is 3.73 m/s², Earth's 9.80 m/s²: 3.73 / 9.80 = 0.38. NASA Mars Fact Sheet: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/marsfact.html
arrival._survey_readme: UPGRADE_PLAN_V6 C4 (2026-11-15): three dig sites, three ice samples, one at a time. Walking onto a site reads the ground radar (story.json arrival_screen > survey). Deeper ice = a longer drill hold (fill_seconds); farther sites = a longer run back to the analyzer before the ice turns to gas. text_as = the task uses that task's words; site = the number shown in the task list. Depths, positions, fill_seconds and data_gb: PLACEHOLDER: game-design choice. The idea that radar finds buried ice: NASA MRO SHARAD (see twins in this file).

list.text: MRO's HiRISE camera takes very sharp pictures of Mars from orbit.

list.text: MRO's SHARAD radar looks under the surface of Mars for buried ice.
list.source: NASA: MRO's ground-penetrating radar found buried ice under Utopia Planitia: https://science.nasa.gov/photojournal/scalloped-terrain-led-to-finding-of-buried-ice-on-mars/

list.text: In 2008 the Phoenix lander dug into the soil near Mars's north pole and found water ice.

orbit.reason: Nobody lands on Venus. Too hot: the ground would melt lead.
orbit.source: NASA Venus facts: the surface is about 872 F (467 C), "hot enough to melt lead", and the longest lander survived about two hours: https://science.nasa.gov/venus/venus-facts/

list.text: In 1985 two Soviet VEGA balloons floated in the clouds of Venus.
list.source: NASA NSSDCA, Vega 1 Balloon (released 11 June 1985, floated at about 54 km): https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=1984-125F
